To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) swinger transformations are a unique method to detect unknown RNAs from NGS; (ii) swinger transformations are used to identify putative non-coding RNA transcribed regions; (iii) swinger transformation occurs mainly on highly transcribed genes; (iv) swinger-transcribed genes are associated with cancer; and (v) swinger transformation is an efficient method to identify noncoding RNAs.
swinger transformation of ESTs is a unique method for identifying noncanonical RNAs and putative transcription of ncRNA regions, and swinger-transcribed genes associate with cancer progression.
swinger transformation of expressed sequences identifies putative transcription of non-coding regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of unknown RNAs in normal and cancer cell transcriptomes.
the identification of unknown ESTs, which are assumed artefacts or sequencing errors.
the identification of the origin and function of unknown RNAs, and the development of new computational methods to study them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
swinger transformations identify unknown RNA transcripts from non-coding regions of the genome.
swinger RNAs are transcribed from highly active genes irrespectively of their coding status.

swinger RNAs are a new category of RNAs that are not artefacts, and that are transcribed from non-coding genomic regions, and from protein coding genes, and that are present in normal and cancer cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 347 unknown EST from the FAPSEP/LICR Human Genome Cancer Project were not artefacts but real RNAs, which were not identified due to lack of sequence similarity with template DNA.

the systematic nucleotide exchange analysis is a unique method of identifying noncanonical RNAs and their transcription regions, and that the systematic nucleotides exchanges occur in highly active genes, both in normal and cancer cells.
the 10 identified swinger-transcribed genes associate with cancer induction, progression, and metastasis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the systematic nucleotide exchange approach, called swinger transformation, is a powerful method for identifying noncanonical RNAs and their transcriptional origins.
swinger transformation is a unique and powerful method to identify non-coding RNAs from next generation sequencing.
the human genome contains many non-coding regions that are transcribed.
